newsitem.title: FRANCE: France shows will to qualify for EMU - economists.
newsitem.headline: France shows will to qualify for EMU - economists.

text.p: France's new Socialist-led government has shown its determination to qualify for European monetary union with its emergency 1997 deficit-cutting package, boosting taxes on big business, economists said on Monday.
The decision to increase corporate taxes but spare ordinary taxpayers from the measures means France's fragile economic recovery would not be jeopardised, they said.

But to keep the deficit down in the longer term, the government will have to attack the structural roots of France's budget problems and reform the pension and health care systems, as well as reducing the size of the civil service, they added.

Finance Minister Dominique Strauss-Kahn announced measures on Monday to cut the deficit by 32 billion francs ($5.3 billion) and keep France on course for the single currency after a government-ordered audit found the 1997 budget shortfall running at 3.5 to 3.7 percent of gross domestic product (GDP).
That is well above the three percent target set in the Maastricht treaty on monetary union.
The plan involves 22 billion francs in extra taxes on profits and capital gains of firms with turnover above 50 billion francs and 10 billion francs in spending cuts.
Corporate taxes on the 20 percent of companies affected by the government's measures were pushed up by 15 percent to 41 percent, more than the 10 percent initially expected.
"They've shown their determination to move toward monetary union and the decision to raise corporate taxes will not constrain the economy," said Deutsche Bank's Patrick Mange.
"But they cannot keep using these cosmetic measures to cut the deficit. They must undertake fundamental reforms."
Christopher Potts, economist at brokerage Chevreux de Virieu, agreed the new measures should allay fears about France's commitment to joining monetary union at its planned launch in 1999.
"There's no government in this country which is going to say 'no' to EMU," he said.
Shares lost ground on the rise in corporate taxes but bonds were largely unaffected by the package, which was leaked to the media, and the franc firmed slightly against the mark.
"The bond market is looking at the bottom line, which is whether monetary union will be achieved and it believes it will be," said one economist.

While Strauss-Kahn would not specify a deficit target for 1997, he said the measures were aimed at shaving 0.4 of a percentage point off the deficit and the gap would hit three percent in 1998. It was 4.1 percent in 1996.

Economists predicted that Germany would accept a French 1997 deficit of 3.2 or 3.3 percent. Despite Germany's assertions to the contrary, its weak economic performance meant its deficit would end up at around the same level, several said.
In any event, "monetary union is not going to be abandoned because one country is a couple of points above three percent," said Mange. "Everyone knows there is a margin," said Potts.
The government's decision not to touch household revenues was good news as "it could have been very damaging for consumption," said Hugue de Montvallon of brokerage Oddo.
But he expressed concern that the government would rescind its pledge to cut corporate taxes again in 1999. "These things in France have a worrying tendency to become permanent," he said.
But economists said the government's scope for action had been sharply curtailed by its electoral promises to boost consumption and put France's jobless back to work.
Any switch in priorities would have angered its Communist coalition allies and upset voters who have memories of the U-turn performed by the previous centre-right administration ousted on June 1.
The Socialists campaigned on a pledge of no new austerity to achieve the three percent Maastricht target. ($ = 6.041 French Francs)
